lesson.title: Beyond the Vote: Second-Wave Feminism
lesson.summary: Building on the earlier fight for suffrage, second-wave feminism emerged in the 1960s to challenge workplace discrimination, narrow gender roles, and unequal legal treatment of women, drawing both energy and legal tools from the civil rights movement unfolding alongside it.
lesson.body:
The "first wave" of American feminism had focused above all on winning women the right to vote, a fight won with the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. For decades afterward, organized feminist activism receded from national politics even as many inequalities in pay, employment, education, and legal status remained largely unaddressed.

Renewed feminist activism, later called second-wave feminism, began building through the early 1960s. A key catalyst was Betty Friedan's 1963 book The Feminine Mystique, which challenged the widespread postwar assumption that suburban domesticity was the natural and sufficient fulfillment of a woman's life, giving voice to what Friedan called "the problem that has no name," the quiet dissatisfaction felt by many women, especially educated ones, confined largely to housework and childrearing.

The movement gained an unexpected legal tool from the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Its Title VII, which banned employment discrimination, included "sex" among the protected categories alongside race, color, religion, and national origin. Feminist activists seized on Title VII to challenge sex discrimination in hiring and pay, and in 1966 Friedan and other activists founded the National Organization for Women, in part to pressure the newly created Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to actually enforce the law's ban on sex discrimination.

Over the following years, second-wave feminists pursued a wide range of goals: equal pay, an end to hiring discrimination, access to birth control, and reproductive rights, an area where the Supreme Court's 1973 decision in Roe v. Wade became a major landmark. Title IX, passed in 1972, banned sex discrimination in federally funded education programs. Feminist organizers also pushed for an Equal Rights Amendment to the Constitution, which passed Congress in 1972 but ultimately fell short of ratification by the required number of states.

Like the civil rights movement it ran alongside and often borrowed strategies from, second-wave feminism was never a single, unified organization. It was a broad and sometimes internally divided current that encompassed legal reform efforts, grassroots consciousness-raising groups, and more radical critiques of gender roles in American society altogether.
